analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose and limit workplace surveillance of workers, and bans selling worker data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in any of the three committees it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers to tell workers in plain language what surveillance they are under — emails, location tracking, keystrokes, cameras, biometric scans — and how that data is used in decisions about pay, scheduling, and firing. It would have banned the most intrusive practices: monitoring workers off-duty or in restrooms and locker rooms, using surveillance to identify union activity or whistleblowers, and selling workers' data. It created a new enforcement office at the Labor Department and let workers sue with statutory damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 11 or more employees — including applicants, gig and contract workers, federal and state employees, and congressional staff — would gain the right to know what data their employer collects about them, correct inaccurate data, and be told when a surveillance system drove a decision about their job. Unions would gain protection against surveillance used to identify organizing. Workers suing under the bill could not be forced into predispute arbitration or to waive class actions, and prevailing workers and unions could recover up to treble damages plus attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must disclose in plain language what workplace surveillance they conduct, what data is collected, how, how often, and how it affects performance and productivity assessments, and workers must acknowledge receipt [S2].

Workers can request all surveillance data collected on them within 7 days and have incomplete or erroneous data corrected, and must be told within 7 days when an employment decision was made using surveillance data [S2].

The bill bans using surveillance to identify union organizing or protected concerted activity, to monitor off-duty workers or sensitive areas like restrooms and lactation rooms, to track health or disability status unrelated to the job, or to identify workers reporting violations of law [S2].

Employers may not sell or license workers' data, may not collect data unrelated to business operations, and may not transfer personally identifiable data to third parties unless the worker is told, given encryption protections, and does not opt out [S2].

Workers and unions get a private right of action with statutory damages (up to $20,000 per violation, up to $40,000 willful; retaliation up to $50,000–$100,000), attorney's fees, and immunity from predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers [S2].
The bill bars employers from retaliating against workers who complain, cooperate with investigations, or testify about surveillance violations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more employees — including public agencies — bear the cost of documenting and disclosing every surveillance practice, honoring data access and correction requests, restricting data collection to what is operationally necessary, and rewriting vendor contracts. Companies selling workplace monitoring software and data services lose a market for off-duty tracking, data sales, and opaque scoring. The bill also creates a new Labor Department division at taxpayer expense.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers and surveillance tech vendors

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on employers of almost any size — the threshold is just 11 employees — requiring written disclosures, acknowledgments, data-access systems, and vendor contract rewrites that small businesses would feel most [S2].

The private right of action carries statutory damages with no proof of harm and treble damages, which good-faith critics would say invites litigation over paperwork violations; the bill does guard against this with a 60-day notice window for regulators to intervene first [S2].

Employers argue some monitoring is legitimate for security, safety, and quality control; the bill's carve-outs are limited, and its definitions of 'data' and 'workplace surveillance' are broad enough to reach ordinary HR files, customer-interaction ratings, and infectious-disease screening information, which could create compliance uncertainty [S2].

Creating a new Privacy and Technology Division inside the Labor Department, with a presidentially appointed administrator and four advisory boards, adds a permanent federal bureaucracy whose cost and effectiveness the bill does not cap or test [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and increasingly urgent: employers can already track workers' keystrokes, locations, and off-duty lives with little notice, and the bill would give workers basic transparency, a right to correct false data, and protection against surveillance aimed at union activity and whistleblowers. The costs are genuine but conventional — compliance burden on employers down to 11 employees, litigation risk from statutory damages, and a new agency — and the bill mitigates the litigation risk with notice and intervention procedures. On balance it is a substantive worker-privacy floor whose main design question is how broadly the definitions sweep.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced and none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Deluzio introduced the Stop Spying Bosses Act on March 15, 2024, with Rep. Bonamici as the bill's sole cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].

The Speaker referred it to three committees — Education and the Workforce, Oversight and Accountability, and House Administration — for consideration of provisions in each committee's jurisdiction [S4].
No committee took any further action: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote appear in the bill's action history through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that monitor workers and the companies selling workplace surveillance technology are better off, because no disclosure, data-access, or off-duty-monitoring restrictions were enacted and the status quo continues.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require disclosure of workplace surveillance, ban monitoring of off-duty workers and union activity, and let workers sue over violations [S1][S2].

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction [S3].

against.name: House committee leadership (Education and the Workforce; Oversight and Accountability; House Administration)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the sole cosponsor was a Democrat, with no Republican support in the record; the Republican-led House took no action on the bill after referral [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and employee-monitoring technology vendors
industries.note: The bill would bar the core of their offering — off-duty tracking, biometric monitoring in sensitive areas, data sales to third parties, and undisclosed AI scoring of workers — and hold employers liable for vendor violations, directly cutting revenue from these services [S2].

industries.industry: Employers with 11 or more employees (including large retailers, logistics, and public agencies)
industries.note: They would bear disclosure, record-keeping, data-access, and vendor-contract costs, and lose the ability to monitor off-duty workers or sell worker data — but transparent practices that workers can verify could also reduce disputes [S2].

industries.industry: Data brokers and third-party data buyers
industries.note: The bill flatly prohibits selling or licensing worker data collected through surveillance, cutting off a market for employee information [S2].

Unions gain a ban on surveillance used to identify organizing, their own right to sue violators, guaranteed seats on the bill's advisory boards, and protection from arbitration and class-action waivers in these disputes [S2].
